stage1_evidence_shown.label: INTRODUCTION
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Patients transported by helicopter often require advanced airway management. The purpose of this study was to determine whether or not the in-flight environment of air medical transport in a BO-105 helicopter impairs the ability of flight nurses to perform oral endotracheal intubation.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: SETTING
stage1_evidence_shown.context: The study was conducted in an MBB BO-105 helicopter.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: METHODS
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Flight nurses performed three manikin intubations in each of the two study environments: on an emergency department stretcher and in-flight in the BO-105 helicopter.

stage2_added_evidence.label: RESULTS
stage2_added_evidence.context: The mean time required for in-flight intubation (25.9 +/- 10.9 seconds) was significantly longer than the corresponding time (13.2 +/- 2.8 seconds) required for intubation in the control setting (ANOVA, F = 38.7, p<.001). All intubations performed in the control setting were placed correctly in the trachea; there were two (6.7%) esophageal intubations in the in-flight setting. The difference in appropriate endotracheal intubation between the two settings was not significant (chi 2 = 0.3; p>0.05).
